title: Theophany: blessing the waters
hookLine: Orthodox priests throw a cross into rivers and sea, and swimmers dive for it

lines: THE CROSS SPINS OUT OVER THE WATER.
cards: A crowd packs the edge of a harbor on a January morning. Young men stand along the dock in swim shorts, shivering, eyes on a priest in gold vestments holding up a wooden cross.

The priest throws the cross, spinning, out over the water. It lands with a splash, and the swimmers hit the water after it. One comes up holding it over his head, soaked and grinning, and the crowd cheers.
It happens in Greek towns, in Orthodox parishes by rivers and lakes, and on seashores far from Greece.

teach.b: Theophany means God appearing, God made visible. For Orthodox and other Eastern Christians, it's a great January feast, and it remembers one scene above all: the baptism of Jesus in the river Jordan.

teach.h: THE SON, THE SPIRIT, THE VOICE.
teach.b: Matthew tells it: "And Jesus, when he was baptized, went up straightway out of the water: and, lo, the heavens were opened unto him, and he saw the Spirit of God descending like a dove, and lighting upon him: And lo a voice from heaven, saying, This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."
Look at who is there. The Son in the river, the Spirit like a dove, the Father's voice from heaven. Eastern Christians see the Trinity shown in one moment, at a riverbank.
Then the turn that explains the harbor.

teach.h: NOT TO BE CLEANSED, BUT TO BLESS.
teach.b: Orthodox Christians teach that Jesus didn't go into the Jordan to be made clean.
He went in to make the water holy, so that all water, every river, every sea, could carry blessing. So on this day the priest blesses water, often outdoors, at a river, lake or sea.
Families carry bottles of it home, drink a little, sprinkle their rooms, and keep some for the year.
The cross thrown into the harbor acts it out: it goes down into the water, the way Christ went down into the Jordan, and comes back up. A psalm says: "The voice of the LORD is upon the waters."
Western churches remember the baptism too, soon after Epiphany; the Eastern feast blesses the water itself.

how: On Theophany, Orthodox and other Eastern churches celebrate the Great Blessing of the Waters, in church and often outdoors at a river, lake or sea, where a cross may be thrown in and retrieved by swimmers; families take blessed water home.

o: God made visible, at Jesus's baptism in the Jordan
the day Jesus rose into heaven before his friends

games.q: you're standing on the riverbank as Jesus comes up out of the Jordan. what does Matthew say happens next?
o: the crowd cheers and the disciples gather.
the heavens open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and a voice speaks.
nothing at all; he walks away in silence.
games.why: the heavens open, the Spirit comes down like a dove, and a voice says, "This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased."

practice: Pour a glass of water and hold it in both hands: water you didn't make, that fell as rain somewhere and ran through rivers and pipes to reach you.

If you pray, you can trace a cross over it, as some Orthodox families do with the water they bring home, and give thanks in the psalm's words, the voice of the Lord is upon the waters; if you don't, simply be thankful for it.

wordCard.voice: Theophany. God made visible: the Eastern feast of Christ's baptism in the Jordan, when the waters are blessed and the cross is thrown into the sea.

orig.note: Greek: Theophany — the Eastern name for the feast of Christ's baptism, God appearing.

carryVoice: Your line: the waters blessed. Every river, every sea. Until next time.
